Abstract heading

spans.assertion: the analysis found no statistically significant conditional correlation between skin tone and red-card issuance

spans.note: states the research's primary intent is to take part in the crowdstorming exercise, not to establish the existence or causality of referee bias
One Sentence Summary heading

spans.assertion: used a linear probability model for the analysis
found no statistically significant conditional correlation between skin tone and red-card issuance

spans.note: Results section heading
frames the central research questions: whether referees give more red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players, and whether that varies with the referee's home-country prejudice
asserts the data are not sufficient to determine whether the bias exists or its magnitude, due to confounding variables, making conclusions difficult

spans.assertion: concludes that a player's skin color does not affect the likelihood of being issued a red card

spans.note: lays out a conceptual decomposition of red-card probability into infraction, observation, and issuance probabilities, and notes bias could manifest as reduced observation effort or increased leniency

spans.assertion: states the analysis is unable to disentangle whether referee bias manifests through reduced observation effort versus leniency in enforcement

spans.note: argues infraction rates are themselves endogenous to expected detection, which would temper or reverse any observed red-card bias
sets out an assumption that referees treat skin color as a signal of infraction likelihood, weakening as referees observe a player repeatedly

spans.assertion: restricted the sample to player-referee dyads with only a single interaction, to limit confounding from referees updating beliefs over repeated observations
did not account for changes in team strategy from opponent pairings, since the unit of analysis is player-referee rather than player-game-referee observations

spans.note: acknowledges this is an unrealistic assumption but says it is necessitated by the data available

spans.assertion: the primary empirical analysis is a linear probability model of red-card incidence on player skin tone and, depending on specification, player characteristics (height, weight, age) and club fixed effects
included an indicator variable for each rater's skin-tone classification category to capture non-linear effects
Table 1 shows results using rater 1's classifications in columns 1-2 and rater 2's classifications in columns 3-4
assumed that referees do not issue red cards unless a player commits an infraction
clustered t-statistics/standard errors at the referee's home-country level to account for common training among referees from the same country
defined the category-1 (darkest) indicator as the difference in red-card probability between the lightest- and darkest-skinned players
found this darkest-vs-lightest probability difference was not statistically significant at conventional levels in any specification
concluded there is no basis to reject the null hypothesis that referees are unbiased — skin tone does not change the marginal probability of a red card

chose to keep using a linear probability model rather than a non-linear model, because LPM's indicator variables for club and position remove unobserved category-invariant confounders, a property not guaranteed for non-linear models
constructed an odds ratio at the request of the organizing authors, to enable comparison across research teams
defined the odds ratio as the odds of a red card for a category-1 (darkest) player relative to the odds for a category-0 (lightest) player

computed the odds ratio by predicting each player's red-card probability from player characteristics, then averaging predicted probabilities within category 1 and separately within category 0 (the omitted/reference category) to get each group's conditional probability
calculated an odds ratio of 1.283
created an interaction between a dummy for referees from above-mean-IAT-score countries (high IAT) and the categorical skin-tone indicator, to test whether bias is concentrated in high-IAT referees
Table 2 presents these interaction results with rater 1's classifications in columns 1-2 and rater 2's in columns 3-4
found these results do not support the conclusion that referee bias is more prevalent among referees with high implicit-bias (IAT) scores

repeated the same procedure for explicit bias: created a dummy (high Exp) for referees from countries with an above-mean explicit-bias score, and interacted it with the categorical skin-tone indicator
states that these results (from the explicit-bias interaction test) do not support the conclusion that referee bias is more prevalent in referees with high IAT, as literally written

Tables 4 through 6 repeat the Table 1-3 analyses but exclude 'club' as an explanatory variable, at the request of the project organizers due to some concern about how the club variable was constructed
notes that the odds-ratio calculation method is mechanically invariant to model choice, because it relies on a linear probability model
found that omitting the club fixed effect does not change the analysis's conclusions

spans.note: 'Change in Analysis Strategy' section heading

spans.assertion: did not change the analysis strategy between the first and second round of the project
declined to reverse the removal of repeat player-referee observations, holding stronger concerns about the endogeneity of player strategy than the comments received

kept the linear probability model despite it not respecting 0/1 probability bounds, rather than switching to a non-linear model, because LPM's indicators still cleanly remove category-invariant characteristics — a property not guaranteed for non-linear models

spans.note: Conclusion heading (precedes Table 1 in the document layout)

spans.assertion: Table 1 presents a regression of an indicator for a player being issued a red card on indicators for the player's skin-tone category plus control variables
the t-statistics in Table 1 are clustered at the referee's country level

Table 1 shows none of the skin-tone category indicators (0.25, 0.50, 0.75, or darkest=1) has a statistically significant coefficient in any of the four specifications, with an adjusted R² near zero, for a sample of 62,310 players
concludes the evidence does not support an economically meaningful skin-tone-based bias in referees' red-card decisions
